section.title: The Scroll Burned by Jehoiakim
section.sectionRationale: God orders Jeremiah's decades of oracles gathered onto a single scroll, one last appeal to a nation and a king who still might turn. Baruch reads it in the temple, then before the officials, then before King Jehoiakim himself, who slices the scroll apart column by column and feeds it to the fire in his winter room. The chapter turns on what happens next: God simply orders it written again, longer than before, with judgment now added on the king who tried to destroy it.
section.thesis: Jehoiakim can burn the parchment but not the word: he cuts and burns every column without fear, yet God commands the scroll rewritten and enlarged and pronounces personal judgment on the very king who tried to silence it, proving that His spoken word outlasts every attempt to destroy it.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: the scroll commanded and written at Jeremiah's dictation; Baruch reading it in the temple and then before the officials; Jehoiakim burning it column by column in his winter quarters; and the scroll rewritten, with judgment now pronounced on the king himself.

units.label: The scroll commanded and written
units.note: one last appeal before the disaster

verses.text: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD:
“Take a {{megillah|scroll}} and write on it all the words I have spoken to you concerning Israel, Judah, and all the nations, from the day I first spoke to you during the reign of Josiah until today.
Perhaps when the people of Judah hear about all the calamity I plan to bring upon them, each of them will {{shuv|turn}} from his wicked way. Then I will forgive their iniquity and their sin.”
So Jeremiah called Baruch son of Neriah, and at the dictation of Jeremiah, Baruch wrote on a scroll all the words that the LORD had spoken to Jeremiah.
Then Jeremiah commanded Baruch, “I am restricted; I cannot enter the house of the LORD;

so you are to go to the house of the LORD on a day of fasting, and in the hearing of the people you are to read the words of the LORD from the scroll you have written at my dictation. Read them in the hearing of all the people of Judah who are coming from their cities.
Perhaps they will bring their petition before the LORD, and each one will turn from his wicked way; for great are the anger and fury that the LORD has pronounced against this people.”
So Baruch son of Neriah did everything that Jeremiah the prophet had commanded him. In the house of the LORD he read the words of the LORD from the scroll.

units.label: Read in the temple, then before the officials
units.note: the word spreads from the assembly to the palace

verses.text: Now in the ninth month of the fifth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah, a fast before the LORD was proclaimed to all the people of Jerusalem and all who had come there from the cities of Judah.

From the chamber of Gemariah son of Shaphan the scribe, which was in the upper courtyard at the opening of the New Gate of the house of the LORD, Baruch read from the scroll the words of Jeremiah in the hearing of all the people.
When Micaiah son of Gemariah, the son of Shaphan, heard all the words of the LORD from the scroll,

he went down to the scribe's chamber in the king's palace, where all the officials were sitting: Elishama the scribe, Delaiah son of Shemaiah, Elnathan son of Achbor, Gemariah son of Shaphan, Zedekiah son of Hananiah, and all the other officials.
And Micaiah reported to them all the words he had heard Baruch read from the scroll in the hearing of the people.

Then all the officials sent word to Baruch through Jehudi son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Cushi, saying, “Bring the scroll that you read in the hearing of the people, and come here.” 
So Baruch son of Neriah took the scroll and went to them.

“Please sit down,” they said, “and read it in our hearing.” 
So Baruch read it in their hearing.
When they had heard all these words, they turned to one another in fear and said to Baruch, “Surely we must report all these words to the king.”
“Tell us now,” they asked Baruch, “how did you write all these words? Was it at Jeremiah's dictation?”
“It was at his dictation,” Baruch replied. “He recited all these words to me and I wrote them in ink on the scroll.”
Then the officials said to Baruch, “You and Jeremiah must hide yourselves and tell no one where you are.”

units.label: Jehoiakim burns the scroll
units.note: a king cuts and burns what he will not obey

verses.text: So the officials went to the king in the courtyard. And having stored the scroll in the chamber of Elishama the scribe, they reported everything to the king.
Then the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll, and he took it from the chamber of Elishama the scribe. And Jehudi read it in the hearing of the king and all the officials who were standing beside him.
Since it was the ninth month, the king was sitting in his winter quarters with a fire burning before him.
And as soon as Jehudi had read three or four columns, Jehoiakim would cut them off with a scribe's knife and throw them into the firepot, until the entire scroll had been consumed by the fire.
Yet in hearing all these words, the king and his servants did not become frightened or tear their garments.
Even though Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah urged the king not to burn the scroll, he would not listen to them.

Instead, the king commanded Jerahmeel, a son of the king, as well as Seraiah son of Azriel and Shelemiah son of Abdeel, to seize Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet. But the LORD had hidden them.

units.label: The word rewritten and Jehoiakim judged
units.note: fire cannot destroy what God has spoken

verses.text: After the king had burned the scroll containing the words that Baruch had written at Jeremiah's dictation, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:
“Take another scroll and rewrite on it the very words that were on the original scroll, which Jehoiakim king of Judah has burned.

You are to proclaim concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah that this is what the LORD says: You have burned the scroll and said, ‘Why have you written on it that the king of Babylon would surely come and destroy this land and deprive it of man and beast?’
Therefore this is what the LORD says about Jehoiakim king of Judah: He will have no one to sit on David's throne, and his body will be thrown out and exposed to heat by day and frost by night.

I will punish him and his descendants and servants for their iniquity. I will bring on them, on the residents of Jerusalem, and on the men of Judah, all the calamity about which I warned them but they did not listen.”

Then Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to the scribe Baruch son of Neriah, and at Jeremiah's dictation he wrote on it all the words of the scroll that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire. And many similar words were added to them.

megillah.gloss: A scroll, a rolled sheet of leather or papyrus for writing. God commands decades of oracles gathered onto a single scroll as one last, comprehensive appeal, so that the whole weight of the warning could be heard and read at once rather than piecemeal.

shuv.gloss: To turn or return, the Old Testament's ordinary word for repentance. The scroll is written and read for exactly this purpose, that hearing all the warnings together might turn even one wicked heart back to the LORD before disaster falls.

basic.context: God tells Jeremiah to gather everything he has preached since the days of Josiah onto one scroll, one final, comprehensive appeal before disaster falls. Baruch writes it and reads it publicly, first in the temple, then before the royal officials, who are alarmed enough to warn Baruch and Jeremiah to hide. When King Jehoiakim hears it read, he calmly slices off each column with a scribe's knife and burns it in his fire pot, unmoved and unafraid. God's response is to have it rewritten, longer than before, with a specific judgment now added on Jehoiakim himself.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a narrative about the nature of God's word, not merely about one scroll: read literally, it teaches that God's spoken word is durable in a way physical documents are not. Jehoiakim's calm, methodical burning contrasts sharply with the officials' fear, showing hardened unbelief can sit undisturbed in the very presence of a clear warning. The scroll's rewriting, expanded rather than diminished, is the chapter's real punch line.
basic.originalLanguages: The megillah, scroll, is simply the physical medium, a rolled sheet that can be cut and burned column by column. The purpose of writing it is that people might shuv, turn, from their wicked way. The knife that cuts the scroll and the fire that consumes it stand for every human power raised against God's revealed word, and both fail to accomplish what the king intends.
basic.typology: The king's knife and fire, wielded against a written word that keeps returning in fuller form, anticipates the far greater hostility later raised against the Word made flesh, and the same pattern of apparent defeat followed by vindication.
basic.christ: Isaiah had already said the word of our God stands forever, and Jesus later says heaven and earth will pass away but His words will never pass away. Jehoiakim's burned and rewritten scroll is a small, vivid enactment of that truth: human power can destroy parchment but not the word itself. The pattern reaches its fullest expression when the Word made flesh is put to death and buried, yet rises, His word and His person both proved indestructible.
basic.god: God is patient, sending a final, gathered appeal in hope that even now the nation might repent, and He forgives readily wherever people turn. Yet He is not mocked: when the king answers mercy with contempt, cutting and burning what he refuses to obey, God simply restores His word in fuller form and adds a specific, personal judgment on the one who tried to destroy it.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 40:8 says the word of our God stands forever. Matthew 24:35 has Jesus say heaven and earth will pass away but His words will never pass away. Psalm 2 shows kings taking counsel together against the LORD and being answered from heaven. 1 Peter 1:24-25 quotes Isaiah to the same effect, that the word of the Lord endures forever.
basic.oneStory: The scroll burned by Jehoiakim is a small, concrete picture of a truth that runs through the whole Bible: every human attempt to silence God's word only proves its indestructibility, since God simply speaks it again, fuller than before, until it reaches its final form in Christ, the Word who was put to death and rose.

context.literary:
Jeremiah 36 sits at the hinge of the book. Its date, the fourth year of Jehoiakim, is the same year given in Jeremiah 25:1, 45:1 and 46:2, and the chapters that follow (37 to 45) are arranged by the prophet's story rather than by the calendar. The scroll gathers up the preaching that came before; what comes after is the cost of having preached it.

The chapter is built in four panels that mirror one another. The command to write (verses 1 to 8) is answered by the command to write again (verses 27 to 32). The public reading, first to the people and then to the officials (verses 9 to 19), is answered by the king's reading and burning (verses 20 to 26). In the first panel God speaks with a 'perhaps,' verses 3 and 7. In the last He speaks with a 'therefore,' verse 30. The hope that the scroll might work is spent, and a verdict takes its place.

The scroll is heard three times, each time nearer to power. Baruch reads to the crowd in the temple court, verse 10, then to the officials in the scribe's chamber of the palace, verse 15, and finally the scroll is read to the king in his winter quarters, verse 21. The reader changes at the last step. Baruch is never brought before Jehoiakim; a royal servant, Jehudi, reads, and the king hears the word of God only through his own courtier. The phrase 'in the hearing of' returns again and again, verses 6, 10, 13, 14, 15 and 21, so that the chapter is about hearing, and about what hearing does and does not produce.

The narrator also stages two reactions side by side. The officials 'turned to one another in fear,' verse 16, while the king and his servants 'did not become frightened or tear their garments,' verse 24. Behind the second sentence stands another king, Josiah, who tore his clothes when Shaphan read him the Book of the Law, 2 Kings 22:11. The reader is meant to hear that scene and feel its absence. The burning itself is told in a measured, repeated rhythm, a few columns read, a cut, a throw into the fire, until the last strip is gone, verse 23.
context.historical:
In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar broke the Egyptian army at Carchemish, and the balance of power in the Near East shifted in a season. Jehoiakim owed his throne to Egypt: Pharaoh Neco had made him king in place of his brother and changed his name, 2 Kings 23:34. He then had to change masters, and 2 Kings 24:1 says he served Nebuchadnezzar for three years before rebelling. The Babylonian Chronicle records that in the winter of 604 Nebuchadnezzar's army took Ashkelon, a Philistine city within a few days' march of Jerusalem. A fast proclaimed in the ninth month of the fifth year, verse 9, fits a nation that could hear the war coming.

Jehoiakim was no Josiah. Jeremiah 22:13-17 describes him building a spacious palace of cedar and vermilion with unpaid labour, while his father Josiah had administered justice and taken up the cause of the poor. Jeremiah 26:20-23 records that he hunted down the prophet Uriah son of Shemaiah, had him brought back from Egypt and killed. A king like that does not take a scroll that threatens him lightly.

The scene is drawn from the machinery of a royal court. There is a chamber for scribes in the palace, a named chief scribe, Elishama, and a body of officials who sit together in it, verse 12. Baruch himself came from a family of rank, for his brother Seraiah served as quartermaster, Jeremiah 51:59. The names around him show how close the writing came to the centre of government. Gemariah son of Shaphan kept a chamber at the temple's New Gate, and a clay seal impression with a name matching his has been published from excavations in Jerusalem's City of David, along with many others from a burnt archive. Fire is one reason such seals survived: it baked the clay.

Verse 22 notes that it was the ninth month, which fell in the cold, wet part of the year, and that the king sat in his winter quarters. Amos 3:15 knows the same pairing of winter house and summer house among the wealthy. The fire pot was a brazier at the king's feet, and a scroll of papyrus or leather would burn quickly in it.
context.canonical:
The chapter belongs to a larger conversation in Scripture about what a king must do with God's written word. Deuteronomy 17:18-19 commanded that Israel's king write out a copy of the instruction on a scroll, keep it with him, and read from it all his life so that he might learn to fear the LORD. Josiah, who tore his clothes at the reading of the law, is the pattern that law imagined, 2 Kings 22:11. Jehoiakim, who cuts up the scroll with a knife, is its opposite, and Jeremiah 22:15-16 sets the two fathers and sons side by side.

The re-writing echoes an earlier moment of broken words. When Moses shattered the first tablets, God did not abandon the covenant; He told Moses to cut new ones, and He said, 'I will write on them the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke,' Exodus 34:1.

The prophets use the same idea of a word that cannot be stopped. Isaiah 40:8 says the word of our God stands forever, and Isaiah 55:10-11 says that His word will not return to Him empty. Jeremiah knew this from within; he had been told that God put His words in his mouth, Jeremiah 1:9, and he said of them, 'Your words were found, and I ate them,' Jeremiah 15:16. Another scroll, the one he wrote against Babylon, ended its life in the Euphrates, Jeremiah 51:59-64, a deliberate counterpart to the burning in the fire.

The saved scroll shaped what came after. Daniel read the books and understood from Jeremiah that Jerusalem's desolation would last seventy years, Daniel 9:2, and both Chronicles and Ezra say Cyrus acted to fulfil the word of the LORD through Jeremiah, 2 Chronicles 36:21-22 and Ezra 1:1. In the New Testament Jesus says His words will never pass away, Matthew 24:35, and Paul writes from chains that 'the word of God cannot be chained,' 2 Timothy 2:9. The last chapter of the Bible warns against taking away from the words of the book of prophecy, Revelation 22:19, which is what Jehoiakim did column by column.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants readers who have the book of Jeremiah in their hands to understand why they have it. Its words were written down by a scribe because the prophet was shut out of the temple and because God intended His message to outlast the moment, to speak when the prophet could not. Anyone reading Jeremiah after the exile is holding the second scroll of Jeremiah 36:32, enlarged and survived.

The chapter also lays two responses to the same word side by side so that readers can place themselves. The officials hear and are afraid, but they act only to protect the messengers and report to the king. The king hears and is unmoved. Neither group does what verses 3 and 7 asked, which was to turn. The chapter shows that being alarmed is not the same as repenting, and that being reasonable about a message is not the same as obeying it.

Finally the narrator wants Israel to see that the end of the kingdom was not a matter of missing information. A full, written, public warning was given three times in a single winter, and the king heard it all. When the exiles asked why Jerusalem fell, here was part of the answer: the word was read to the throne itself, and the throne took out a knife.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a king burning a prophetic scroll and a prophet having it rewritten; it prescribes neither. Nothing here commands believers to copy the scroll's methods, such as dictating to a scribe, reading on a fast day, or hiding from rulers. Baruch's fast-day reading was Jeremiah's tactical instruction for his own situation, verses 5 to 6.

What the chapter does give for the present is a set of examples. Baruch is the pattern of a faithful transmitter, who does 'everything that Jeremiah the prophet had commanded him,' verse 8, and who risks his freedom to do it. The officials are a warning that private alarm which never becomes public obedience is not enough. And the repeated 'perhaps' of verses 3 and 7 shows how God Himself treats a hearing audience: He sends the message in the hope of its being received, even when it is the last chance.

Care is also needed with verse 30. It is a specific sentence on a specific king, and it should not be turned into a general rule that anyone who opposes God's word will meet the same fate in the same form.

debates.question: What did the first scroll contain, and how does it relate to the book we have?

views.label: Early oracles, now spread through chapters 1 to 25
views.case: God told Jeremiah to write down all he had said about Israel, Judah and the nations from the days of Josiah, verse 2, which is twenty-three years of preaching, Jeremiah 25:3. Many scholars think this scroll lies behind the early part of the book, perhaps with the oracles against the nations later gathered around it, and that the second scroll grew into the collection we read.

views.label: A shorter set of warnings that cannot be recovered
views.case: The text gives no list of contents. A scroll that could be read three times in one day, and by a single reader before the king, was not unreasonably long. On this view the first scroll was a compact collection of calls to repentance, and the book of Jeremiah is a far larger and later work for which the scroll was only the seed.

views.label: The book's own account of itself is enough
views.case: Verse 32 says that 'many similar words were added.' The chapter's interest is not the scroll's table of contents but its survival and growth, and Jeremiah 30:2 shows the same pattern of God asking His prophet to write His words in a book.

debates.bearing: No view can be proved. The safest conclusion is the one the chapter itself draws: what we hold is the word that survived the fire and grew, and its authority rests on God's speaking, not on our ability to reconstruct a first edition.

debates.question: Does the judgment on Jehoiakim in verse 30 conflict with 2 Kings 24, where his son Jehoiachin does reign?

views.label: A loose, strong way of speaking
views.case: Jehoiachin reigned only three months, 2 Kings 24:8, and was taken to Babylon. The threat that Jehoiakim would 'have no one to sit on David's throne' is read as a statement about enduring dynasty, not about the next three months. Jeremiah 22:30 says the same of Jehoiakim's son, that none of his descendants would prosper to sit on David's throne.

views.label: The throne ends in Jehoiakim's line
views.case: After Jehoiachin the throne passed to his uncle Zedekiah, not to a son of Jehoiakim, 2 Kings 24:17. The threat is read as pointing to the end of Jehoiakim's own line as the ruling line, with Zedekiah as a stopgap from a different branch of the family.

views.label: The sentence awaits the Messiah's resolution
views.case: Jeremiah also promises that David will never lack a man to sit on the throne, Jeremiah 33:17, and a righteous Branch, Jeremiah 23:5. On this view the verdicts on Jehoiakim and his son are real, and the promise to David is kept by a different route, through Christ.

debates.bearing: All three agree that the sentence was carried out, and that hope for David's house had to rest on God's promise rather than on Jehoiakim's descendants. That is where the New Testament places it, Luke 1:32-33.

debates.question: Why does Jeremiah dictate the scroll rather than write it himself?

views.label: Practical restriction
views.case: Verse 5 states plainly that Jeremiah was restricted from entering the temple, so Baruch's role as scribe and reader was a practical necessity, not a theological statement about Jeremiah's authority.

views.label: A partnership modeling shared ministry
views.case: The chapter goes out of its way to name Baruch repeatedly and credit his exact obedience, suggesting the narrative also wants readers to see faithful, costly partnership in ministry, since Baruch risks the same danger as Jeremiah for delivering the same word.

debates.bearing: Either way, the word's authority rests in its divine source, not in who physically pens or reads it, and faithful transmission of that word can cost the messenger as much as the original prophet.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word to notice is the small Hebrew particle behind 'Perhaps' in verses 3 and 7, ulay. God, who is not lacking in knowledge, speaks of what may happen if the people hear. It is the same openness found in Jeremiah 26:3, where God says it may be that they will listen and each turn, so that He will relent. This is not uncertainty on God's part but the language of an honest invitation, a door left open that the hearers must choose to walk through. The word God uses of what He intends is also worth hearing. The calamity that He 'plans' in verse 3 comes from a verb for planning or devising, which also gives the word for 'plans' in Jeremiah 29:11, 'plans to prosper you and not to harm you.' The same God who devises disaster in 18:11 devises peace in 29:11; what He devises depends on what the people do with His word.

The promise at the end of verse 3, 'I will forgive their iniquity and their sin,' uses the verb salach, which in the Old Testament is used only with God as the one who forgives. No human being can salach. The same verb stands in the new covenant promise, Jeremiah 31:34, and in 33:8. So the scroll, in its first purpose, is an invitation to the very forgiveness that Jeremiah elsewhere sets at the centre of God's coming covenant.

In verse 23 the king 'would cut them off,' and in verse 24 the king and his servants did not 'tear their garments.' The Hebrew verb for both is the same root, qara, to tear or rend. The same verb narrates Josiah's reaction in 2 Kings 22:11, 'he tore his clothes.' Jehoiakim tears the scroll rather than tearing his clothes. The wordplay does the moral work of the sentence. What should have been torn, the proud heart, is left whole, and what should have been honoured is torn to pieces.

The word rendered 'columns' in verse 23 is literally 'doors,' from the noun delet. A scroll's written panels stood side by side like a row of doors, and the king opens and shuts them one after another with his knife. The picture is of a man destroying the very entrances God had opened.

Hiding gets a pointed treatment. In verse 19 the officials tell Baruch and Jeremiah to 'hide yourselves,' and in verse 26 'the LORD had hidden them.' It is the same root, satar. The officials' advice is carried out by a more reliable guardian. What human prudence recommends, God secures.

Finally, the verb 'hear' is used in the chapter in two quite different ways. The people hear, and the king hears, and everyone is in the 'hearing' of the scroll; the Hebrew idiom in verse 10 is literally 'in the ears of all the people.' But verse 25 says that the king 'would not listen' to Elnathan, Delaiah and Gemariah, and verse 31 says the people 'did not listen.' The root shama bears both meanings, to hear and to obey. In Hebrew thought, hearing that does not become obedience is not completed hearing at all.

typology.type: The second scroll, and the second tablets, Exodus 34:1
typology.fulfillment: When the first tablets were broken, God had them recut and wrote the same words again. When the first scroll was burned, God had it rewritten with added words. In both cases human sin destroys the medium and God keeps the word. The pattern climbs to the new covenant, in which the law is no longer written on stone or on scroll but on 'tablets of human hearts,' 2 Corinthians 3:3, as Jeremiah 31:33 had promised. The type falls short in that both earlier media could be broken or burned, while the Spirit's writing in the heart cannot be reached by a knife.

typology.type: The word cut up and consumed, then restored and enlarged
typology.fulfillment: The scroll is destroyed by those in authority, apparently ending the matter, and then returns fuller than before. Christ is the Word made flesh, John 1:14, and He too was destroyed by those in authority, buried, and raised in greater glory. He had said, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,' John 2:19-21. The escalation is that Jeremiah needed Baruch's pen to restore the scroll, while Christ rose by His own life. The scroll came back with 'many similar words,' but Christ came back as the living end of everything the scroll was pointing to.

The king sent men to seize Baruch and Jeremiah, 'But the LORD had hidden them.' When hostile hearers picked up stones against Jesus, 'Jesus was hidden and went out of the temple area,' John 8:59. Faithful messengers are kept until their work is finished. The correspondence has limits. Baruch and Jeremiah were spared this time and later suffered, while Jesus was kept only until His hour, and then gave Himself up, John 10:17-18. Believers in later centuries who were not hidden, as in Acts 4:18-20 where the apostles refused to stop speaking, remind us that God's protection is sometimes deliverance and sometimes strength to endure.

typology.type: Jehoiakim's line cut off from David's throne, Jeremiah 36:30
typology.fulfillment: The sentence on Jehoiakim and his descendants, with the later word on his son, Jeremiah 22:30, appears to close the door on David's throne. Matthew's genealogy passes through the exile and names Jeconiah, Matthew 1:11-12, and Luke traces another path, Luke 3:23-31. Where the earthly line ran dry, God raised up 'a righteous Branch' for David, Jeremiah 23:5, and the angel says that the Lord God will give Jesus the throne of His father David, Luke 1:32-33. The type falls short because Jehoiakim's judgment concerned one family, while the resolution in Christ rests on God's own promise, not on any king's merit.

study.christ:
The scroll leads to Christ first through the person of the Word. John says that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, John 1:14, and Hebrews says that after speaking to our fathers in many ways through the prophets, God has in these last days spoken by His Son, Hebrews 1:1-2. Jeremiah 36 shows the strain of what the earlier ways of speaking were up against. A written word could be taken to a fire and burned. In Christ the Word is not a thing to be held but a person to be received, and He is not stopped by being killed. The one who was cut off from the land of the living, to use Isaiah's phrase, was raised on the third day.

It also leads to Christ through the offer inside the scroll. The scroll exists so that people would turn and be forgiven, verse 3, and the promise is salach, God's forgiveness. After the resurrection Jesus tells His disciples that 'repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem,' Luke 24:47. The same city that burned the scroll receives the same offer, now sealed in the blood of the One it had rejected. The 'perhaps' of verse 3 becomes a promise in Him.

There is a bitter irony in the other direction. At His trial the high priest tore his clothes, Matthew 26:65. Jehoiakim would not tear his garments at the word of God; Caiaphas tore his in order to condemn the Word of God made flesh. Neither tearing was repentance. The first was a king's refusal to be afraid; the second was an official's pretence of horror that sent the Son to the cross.

The judgment on Jehoiakim's line, and the promise to David that stands in tension with it, lead to Christ as well. The Gospels present Jesus as the Son of David who sits on the throne, Luke 1:32-33, and Revelation shows Him as 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David,' who alone can open the sealed scroll, Revelation 5:5. The God who ordered the first scroll finally entrusts the scroll of history to Christ.

A caution keeps this honest. Jehoiakim is not a picture of Pilate or of Satan, and Baruch is not a picture of the Holy Spirit. The connections above rest on what the New Testament itself says about the word of God, the Son of David and the forgiveness that is preached in His name.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who is persistent in His pursuit of people who have refused Him for twenty-three years. The command to write is not a fresh start but a final gathering up. Behind it stands a history of speaking 'again and again,' Jeremiah 25:3, and now He tries the medium of ink and papyrus, a way of speaking that reaches where the prophet cannot go. It shows His concern that His message reach the people even when its messenger is barred from the temple, verse 5. God does not abandon a hearing because the human instrument is restricted.

The chapter also shows how God holds justice and mercy together. The scroll announces calamity, yet its stated purpose is forgiveness, verse 3. God's threats in Jeremiah are conditional in this sense, as Jeremiah 18:7-8 says plainly: if a nation turns, He will relent. Judgment is what falls on those who will not hear, and mercy is what stands ready for those who will. Verse 7 gives the weight of what is at stake, 'great are the anger and fury that the LORD has pronounced,' and in the same breath keeps a door open, 'perhaps they will bring their petition before the LORD.'

God is sovereign over His word and over the safety of those who carry it. The king commands his own son to seize the prophet and his scribe, 'But the LORD had hidden them,' verse 26. The narrator does not say how. He does not need to. The word and its bearers are in hands that no king commands.

There is a tension the chapter does not resolve. God says 'perhaps' even though He knows, as Jeremiah 7:27 says, that the people will not listen. Both are in Scripture. God's invitations are real, and so is His foreknowledge, and the chapter keeps both without explaining how. The right response is to hear the invitation as sincere and to treat the refusal as the creature's own.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to treasure Scripture, to read it aloud, to fear its warnings and to receive its offers, and to trust that God, who restores what is burned, will keep His word whatever the powers of the day decide to do with it.

crossReferences.note: The mirror scene. Shaphan the scribe reads the Book of the Law to King Josiah, and Josiah tears his clothes and sends to inquire of the LORD. Jehoiakim's court is full of Shaphan's family, and the chapter is built so that the reader hears Josiah's tearing when Jehoiakim refuses to tear.

The king was to copy the law on a scroll, keep it with him and read from it all his life so that he might fear the LORD. Jehoiakim handles a scroll of God's words with a knife, the exact reversal of what the king's own law required of him.

After Moses broke the first tablets, God had them cut again and wrote 'the words that were on the first tablets.' The recovery of a broken word is the closest earlier pattern for the second scroll, and shows that God's faithfulness does not depend on the survival of the medium.

Dated to the same fourth year of Jehoiakim, this summary says the word had come for twenty-three years from Josiah's thirteenth year and that the people had not listened. It gives the span of the preaching that the first scroll was to gather up.

The prophet's portrait of Jehoiakim: building his palace by injustice, while his father Josiah did justice and defended the poor. It supplies the moral background for a king who could hear a warning read and not be afraid.

The earlier fate of the prophet Uriah, whom Jehoiakim had pursued to Egypt and killed. The danger to Baruch and Jeremiah in 36:19 and 36:26 is not an exaggeration, and Elnathan, who fetched Uriah, is among those who plead with the king in 36:25. Ahikam son of Shaphan, whose son is Gedaliah, shielded Jeremiah then.

A word to Baruch dated to the same fourth year, while he was writing at Jeremiah's dictation. It counsels him not to seek great things for himself and promises him his life as a spoil of war wherever he goes, which gives a private, pastoral side to the public drama of chapter 36.

Another scroll, this one of the words against Babylon, read aloud in Babylon and then tied to a stone and cast into the Euphrates. A scroll burned in judgment on Judah's king is matched by a scroll sunk as a sign of judgment on Babylon, and both are God's words.

God's word is likened to rain and snow that do not return without watering the earth, and 'will not return to Me empty.' Jeremiah 36 gives the sentence a narrative: the king's fire cannot make the word return empty, because it comes back in a second scroll.

Daniel, in Babylon, 'understood from the sacred books' the word of the LORD to Jeremiah about seventy years. The rewritten scroll reached the exiles and shaped their prayer, which shows that the word the king burned went on to teach those he exiled.

A closing warning that anyone who takes away from the words of the book of prophecy will lose his share in the tree of life. Jehoiakim removing column after column is the Old Testament picture of what this warning forbids.
Paul, in chains, declares that the word of God cannot be chained. His sentence is Jeremiah 36 in one line: the messenger may be hidden, hunted or imprisoned, but the word still runs.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with God speaking, and a world appearing, Genesis 1. The first human sin is a question about what God said, Genesis 3:1. From that point the story is largely a contest over God's word: whether it will be heard, obeyed, doubted, edited or destroyed. Jehoiakim's knife is one chapter of that contest, and one of its clearest.

Behind the chapter stands Sinai, where God wrote His words on stone and Israel broke the covenant, and where the broken tablets were replaced. Behind it too stands Deuteronomy, which made the written word the centre of Israel's national life and asked the king, above all, to keep it close, Deuteronomy 17:18-19. The kings of Judah are measured by that standard, and the book of Kings keeps score. Josiah tears his clothes and renews the covenant; Jehoiakim cuts the scroll apart. Within a generation Jerusalem falls, and the exiles are left asking why. Jeremiah 36 helps to answer: they were warned in writing, in public, three times in a single winter.

After the exile, the story shows what God did with the word that survived. It was copied, kept and read, until Daniel could set his prayer by it and Ezra and Chronicles could say that Cyrus acted to fulfil it. The scroll that the king could not destroy became part of the canon.

The story reaches its centre in Christ, who is the Word made flesh, and who is put to death by those who hear Him and will not repent. In Him the pattern of the burned and rewritten scroll is lifted into history: the powers destroy what they cannot control, and God raises it again, fuller than before. Then the church carries that word to the nations, hunted and chained at times, and the word is not chained.

The ending of the story gathers what Jeremiah 36 only hinted at. In Revelation a scroll sealed with seven seals is opened by the Lion of Judah, and no one can take a knife to what He unrolls, Revelation 5:5. The book closes with a warning against taking away from the words of prophecy, Revelation 22:19, and with the tree of life open to those who have washed their robes. The 'perhaps' of the first scroll becomes the open door of the last page, and the word that kings tried to burn is the word by which the new creation is spoken into being.

quiz.q: Why does God command Jeremiah to have all his oracles gathered onto one scroll?

options.text: So the people would hear the whole warning at once, and perhaps turn from their wicked ways and be forgiven.
options.note: Verse 3 states this purpose directly, that hearing it might lead each person to repent.

options.text: So the priests would have an official copy for temple records.
options.note: The scroll is read publicly to move hearts to repentance, not filed as an archival record.

options.text: Because Jeremiah could no longer speak and needed a written substitute.
options.note: The text says Jeremiah was restricted from entering the temple, not that he could no longer speak.

options.text: So Baruch could sell copies of the prophecies.
options.note: Baruch does write and read the scroll, but the stated purpose is repentance, not distribution or sale.

quiz.q: How does King Jehoiakim respond when he hears the scroll read?

options.text: He calmly cuts off each column with a scribe's knife and burns it, unafraid, ignoring officials who urge him not to.
options.note: Verses 23 to 25 record his methodical, unmoved destruction of the scroll despite warnings.

options.text: He tears his garments in fear and repents immediately.
options.note: Verse 24 explicitly states neither he nor his servants were frightened or tore their garments.

options.text: He orders the scroll preserved in the temple treasury.
options.note: He does the opposite, destroying the scroll entirely in his fire pot.

options.text: He asks Jeremiah to explain the scroll's meaning before deciding what to do.
options.note: He never consults Jeremiah directly; he sends Jehudi to fetch and read the scroll, then destroys it.

quiz.q: What happens to Baruch and Jeremiah after the scroll is burned?

options.text: The LORD hides them from the king's men sent to seize them.
options.note: Verse 26 states plainly that the LORD had hidden them from Jerahmeel and the others sent to arrest them.

options.text: They are captured and imprisoned immediately.
options.note: The text says the opposite, the LORD hid them from capture.

options.text: They flee to Egypt for permanent safety.
options.note: The chapter does not describe a flight to Egypt; that comes later in the book, after Jerusalem falls.

options.text: They are honored by the king for their honesty.
options.note: The king seeks to seize them, not honor them, after burning their scroll.

quiz.q: What specific judgment does God pronounce on Jehoiakim after the burning?

options.text: He will have no one to sit on David's throne, and his body will be cast out, exposed to heat and frost.
options.note: Verse 30 pronounces this specific, personal judgment naming Jehoiakim directly.

options.text: He will be forgiven since the officials tried to stop him.
options.note: The text pronounces judgment on Jehoiakim personally, despite the officials' efforts.

options.text: His descendants will reign in unbroken peace.
options.note: The judgment says the opposite, no one from his line will sit on David's throne.

options.text: He will be exiled to Babylon in chains like Zedekiah later was.
options.note: The specific judgment given here is about an undignified death and burial, not exile in chains.

quiz.q: What happens to the scroll's content after Jehoiakim burns it?

options.text: Jeremiah dictates it again to Baruch on a new scroll, with many similar words added to it.
options.note: Verse 32 records that the words were rewritten in full, and more were added.

options.text: It is lost forever, since Jehoiakim destroyed the only copy.
options.note: The chapter's whole point is that the word is restored, not lost.

options.text: Only a partial summary is later reconstructed from memory.
options.note: The text says all the former words were rewritten, not merely a partial summary.

options.text: God tells Jeremiah the words no longer need to be written down.
options.note: God commands the opposite, that Jeremiah rewrite the very words that were burned.

questions: Jehoiakim heard the word clearly and destroyed it without fear rather than repenting. Where might you be tempted to dismiss a hard truth from God rather than let it change you?
The officials trembled at the scroll's words while the king did not. What does it look like for you to let conviction actually move you toward God rather than fading into mere alarm?

God's response to the burned scroll was simply to have it rewritten, fuller than before. Where do you need to trust that God's word and God's purposes cannot be undone by opposition or setbacks in your own life?
Baruch risked real danger to write and read faithfully what God had spoken through Jeremiah. Who in your life needs you to pass on a hard but true word, even at some cost to yourself?

This chapter is a small picture of the larger truth fulfilled in Christ, that no human power can finally silence God's word. How does the indestructibility of God's word give you confidence this week?

translationNotes.note: The fifth year of Jehoiakim places this fast in the winter of 604 to 603 BC, likely occasioned by fear after Babylon's recent campaigns in the region, explaining why the people gathered to fast before the LORD.
The scribe's knife used to cut the columns was an ordinary tool for trimming and sharpening reed pens, here turned to the grim purpose of dismembering the scroll piece by piece before burning it.

And many similar words were added to them likely refers to further oracles Jeremiah had delivered in the meantime, or additional detail expanding the original content, showing the second scroll was not merely a copy but an enlargement.
